name: SS-31 (Elamipretide)

b.x: Four amino acids. That is all SS-31 is. D-Arg-dimethylTyr-Lys-Phe-NH2, a tetrapeptide small enough to cross cell membranes without relying on mitochondrial membrane potential. It concentrates more than 1,000-fold inside mitochondria and locks onto cardiolipin, the phospholipid that anchors cytochrome c to the inner mitochondrial membrane. SS-31 (elamipretide, CAS 736992-21-5, also called MTP-131 and Bendavia) earned FDA accelerated approval in September 2025 under the brand name FORZINITY (NDA 215244) for Barth syndrome in patients weighing at least 30 kg. The approval rested on open-label extension data from the TAZPOWER trial (n=12) [1], where knee extensor strength improved 42% from baseline at 168 weeks. The randomized-phase primary endpoints, 6-minute walk test and total fatigue score, were not met in the initial 12-week crossover. Mechanistic evidence is strong. Cardiolipin oxidation collapses cristae, slows electron transfer between complexes III and IV, leaks electrons into superoxide, and drops ATP output. SS-31 prevents that peroxidation; it stabilizes cristae architecture and restores electron flow at the source rather than scavenging free radicals after they form. Preclinical models show reversed age-related cardiac dysfunction [2], improved renal filtration, and neuroprotection from ischemia-reperfusion injury. The longevity community has adopted SS-31 at doses between 2 and 10 mg daily, well below the 40 mg FDA-approved dose. No dose-finding trial exists in healthy adults, so these community doses are pragmatic cost and tolerability decisions rather than clinically validated thresholds. Reports from roughly 50 to 100 threads across r/Peptides, r/longevity, and r/Nootropics describe subtle energy gains, better exercise recovery, and reduced fatigue. Injection site reactions affect nearly all users.

SS-31 is a cell-permeable tetrapeptide with an alternating aromatic-cationic motif. That structure lets it cross lipid bilayers without needing mitochondrial membrane potential as a driving force. Once inside the cell, it accumulates more than 1,000-fold within mitochondria. The target is cardiolipin. This anionic phospholipid sits exclusively on the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it anchors cytochrome c and holds the electron transport chain complexes in their functional supercomplex arrangements. When cardiolipin oxidizes (a consistent hallmark of aging and mitochondrial disease), cristae flatten out. Electron transfer between complexes III and IV slows. Electrons leak sideways to form superoxide. ATP production falls. SS-31 binds directly to cardiolipin and blocks peroxidation. Cristae architecture stays intact. Electron flow through the ETC normalizes. Reactive oxygen species drop at the point of generation, not downstream. The result: improved ATP synthesis, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential, and blocked cytochrome c release, which prevents the intrinsic apoptosis cascade. In aged mice, 8 weeks of SS-31 reversed cardiac diastolic dysfunction and improved contractile reserve [2]. The TAZPOWER open-label extension [1] tracked 12 Barth syndrome patients for 168 weeks and confirmed sustained functional improvements. MMPOWER-3 (n=218) [3] tested SS-31 in primary mitochondrial myopathy; the overall primary endpoint was not met, though a nDNA-variant subgroup showed gains on the 6-minute walk test.
SS-31 benefits center on mitochondrial protection and cellular energy restoration.
Cardiolipin stabilization at the source. SS-31 prevents the lipid peroxidation that collapses cristae and disrupts electron transport, targeting aging where it starts.
42% knee extensor strength increase at 168 weeks in the TAZPOWER open-label extension (n=12 Barth syndrome patients) [1].
Heart protection in preclinical models. Eight weeks of SS-31 reversed diastolic dysfunction in aged mice, restoring cardiac function to near-young levels [2].
Improved exercise recovery reported consistently across community users at 4 to 10 mg daily, with reduced post-workout fatigue and better tolerance during training.
ROS reduction at the electron transport chain rather than downstream scavenging; a mechanistic advantage over conventional antioxidants like vitamin C or CoQ10.
Renal protection in preclinical ischemia-reperfusion models, preserving glomerular filtration through mitochondrial stabilization in kidney tubular cells.

Scientific Evidence
Based on 8 key studies · FDA-approved
FDA accelerated approval granted September 19, 2025 (NDA 215244, FORZINITY) for Barth syndrome: based on open-label extension knee extensor strength improvement, NOT the randomized phase endpoints.
Dosing studied: 40 mg SC once daily (FDA-approved for Barth syndrome); 20 mg for severe renal impairment (eGFR <30, not on dialysis)

The 12-week RCT crossover primary endpoints (6-minute walk test, total fatigue score) were NOT met. MMPOWER-3 Phase 3 (primary mitochondrial myopathy) also failed primary endpoint in the overall population; nDNA-variant subgroup showed 6MWT improvement. No FDA approval for HFpEF or any other indication as of October 2026 (Drugs@FDA). Mechanistic evidence is very strong (cardiolipin stabilization, ROS reduction, ETC restoration). No dose-finding trial in healthy adults exists.
Key Study
PMID 38602181: TAZPOWER 168-week open-label extension (Barth syndrome, n=12); PMID 37268435: MMPOWER-3 Phase 3 (PMM, n=218)
Limitations

Accelerated approval contingent on confirmatory trial verifying clinical benefit. Primary RCT phase of TAZPOWER missed both endpoints. MMPOWER-3 failed overall primary endpoint. All trials conducted in disease populations (Barth syndrome, PMM, HFpEF): no RCT in healthy aging adults. Community doses (1–20 mg) are 2–40× below the studied 40 mg clinical dose with no head-to-head data. Long-term safety beyond 168 weeks unstudied. Phase 3 trial sizes are small (n=12–218) due to orphan-disease context.

b.x: Reconstitution math first, for research-grade powder vials. A 10 mg vial with 1 mL bacteriostatic water gives you 10 mg/mL. At that concentration, 4 mg equals 40 units on a U-100 insulin syringe (0.4 mL). A 10 mg dose takes the full syringe (100 units, 1.0 mL). For the 40 mg vial, add 4 mL BAC water for the same 10 mg/mL concentration; 10 mg is still 100 units, but you get four doses per vial instead of one. FORZINITY, the FDA-approved product, skips all of this. It is a ready-to-use 80 mg/mL solution in a 280 mg/3.5 mL vial (label section 3). Its 40 mg dose is 0.5 mL, drawn with the syringe your healthcare provider prescribes (sections 2.1 and 11, Instructions for Use). Morning dosing is the community standard. There is no meal timing requirement. You'll want to pre-treat injection sites. Cetirizine 10 mg taken 30 minutes before your shot makes a real difference for the first few weeks. Rotate between abdomen and upper thigh, and inject slowly. The site reactions are the number one reason people quit early. Get a CBC at baseline and again at week 8. The eosinophilia is expected, but you want a record showing it was absent before you started. No published stability data exist for reconstituted research-grade SS-31. Community reports keep sealed powder at -20°C and the mixed vial at 2-8°C for up to 28 days. Keep unopened FORZINITY vials at 2-8°C and never freeze them. After the first dose, an opened vial can stay at 2-8°C or at 20-25°C; discard it 8 days after first opening (label section 16.2).
SS-31 (Elamipretide) Cycle

SS-31 does not exhibit receptor desensitization, hormonal axis suppression, or documented antibody formation. Clinical trials used continuous daily dosing for up to 168 weeks (TAZPOWER open-label extension) without cycling. Community cycling (typically 12 weeks on, 4 weeks off) is cost-driven, not biologically required.
No established biological signs of tolerance or receptor downregulation with SS-31
Cost fatigue (≥$150–$300/month at community doses) is the primary practical cycling driver
A planned break after 12–16 weeks can serve as a useful baseline reassessment window
Wash hands thoroughly and clean the vial stopper with an alcohol swab.

Injection site reactions are the defining tolerability challenge with SS-31. In the TAZPOWER trial [4], 100% of participants developed injection site erythema. 75% reported pain. 67% experienced induration. These numbers are not typical for subcutaneous peptides. Community reports confirm the clinical data: redness, swelling, and a firm lump at the injection site are expected, not exceptional. Site rotation between abdomen and upper thigh helps. Reactions typically moderate after 2 to 4 weeks of consistent use. Topical 1% hydrocortisone cream or oral cetirizine 10 mg before injection can reduce severity. Injecting slowly over 30 to 60 seconds also helps based on community experience. If induration expands, feels warm, or shows discharge, stop and evaluate for sterile abscess. Eosinophilia is the second major concern. Raised eosinophil counts are common after 30 or more days of SS-31, with levels peaking around day 90. This shows up on a CBC and can be alarming if unexpected. In elamipretide trials, the rise was not linked to symptoms or other lab changes. Counts returned to baseline after 6 to 12 months of continued use, or after stopping (section 6.1). Do not discontinue solely for isolated eosinophilia without symptoms. If wheeze, GI distress, rash, or other organ-specific symptoms appear alongside raised eosinophils, stop SS-31 and consult a physician immediately. The FORZINITY label carries two warnings (section 5). The first is allergic reactions, including serious ones that needed emergency care, with rash, papular lesions, eczematous dermatitis or cough (section 5.2). They can start anywhere from minutes to months after the first dose. At any sign of an immediate allergic reaction, stop and get medical help right away (section 17). After a serious reaction, the label says not to restart it. Mild to moderate skin reactions can be treated with a topical corticosteroid and an oral antihistamine, though persistent or severe ones may mean stopping. The second warning is benzyl alcohol. FORZINITY contains 20 mg/mL as a preservative, and the label says "Do not use in neonates" (section 5.1). Serious and fatal reactions have been reported in low-birth-weight and preterm newborns given benzyl alcohol-containing drugs intravenously (sections 5.1 and 8.4). Pregnancy and breastfeeding are not contraindications on the FORZINITY label (section 4). Barth syndrome is unlikely to affect females, so there are no data in pregnant women and the risk of birth defects or miscarriage is unknown. Rat and rabbit studies found no harm to development at any dose tested (section 8.1). No data show whether FORZINITY reaches breast milk or affects a breastfed infant. The label weighs breastfeeding's benefits against the mother's need for the drug and any possible harm to the infant (section 8.2). All of this describes FORZINITY; research-grade SS-31 powder is a different product with no safety testing of its own. The MMPOWER-3 trial excluded pregnant or breastfeeding women and required highly effective birth control for women who could become pregnant (NCT03323749). Two cautions here come from research, not the FORZINITY label. People with active cancer should avoid SS-31, since no carcinogenicity studies exist (section 13.1) and MMPOWER-3 excluded active cancer (NCT03323749). That trial also excluded most active cardiac conduction abnormalities, so safety in that group is unknown. Renal impairment matters. SS-31 is renally excreted. The FDA label calls for dose reduction to 20 mg daily for severe renal impairment (eGFR under 30, not on dialysis). Baseline renal function should be checked before starting. Long-term safety beyond 168 weeks has not been characterized. Community users running sub-clinical doses (2 to 10 mg) have less safety data coverage than trial participants at 40 mg. Lower doses likely carry lower risk, but this assumption lacks trial validation.
Common Issues & Solutions

Injection site reactions (erythema, pain, induration): Expected in nearly all users. Apply topical 1% hydrocortisone cream or take cetirizine 10 mg before injection. Reactions typically improve after 2–4 weeks with consistent site rotation (abdomen and upper thigh alternating).

Eosinophilia on CBC: Common after 30+ days; peaks ~day 90. In elamipretide trials, counts returned to baseline after 6 to 12 months of use or after stopping (label section 6.1). Do not discontinue unless accompanied by organ-specific symptoms (wheeze, GI distress, rash). Counts may still be raised at week 16, so repeat the CBC later to track the trend.

No perceived effect at community doses (1–10 mg): Common. Mitochondrial improvements may manifest as subtle energy and recovery changes rather than dramatic subjective effects. Clinical benefit at sub-40 mg doses is not RCT-proven in healthy adults: track objective metrics (exercise performance, HRV, fatigue scores).
High cost / supply interruption: research-grade supply can end partway through a cycle.

Dose confusion (0.5 mg vs 10 mg vs 40 mg): Community uses 0.5–20 mg; the only clinical trial dose was 40 mg/day in disease populations. No validated minimum effective dose for healthy adults. Lower community doses are pragmatic cost/tolerability decisions: not clinically validated efficacy thresholds.
Double-check with AI

Serious hypersensitivity to elamipretide or any FORZINITY excipient: the one contraindication on the FORZINITY label (section 4). Serious allergic reactions needing emergency care have occurred, from minutes to months after starting, and the label says not to restart after one (section 5.2)

Pregnancy and breastfeeding: not a contraindication on the FORZINITY label. The label has no data in pregnant women, so the risk of birth defects or miscarriage is unknown. In rat and rabbit studies, no harm to development occurred at any dose tested (section 8.1). No data show whether it reaches breast milk or affects a breastfed infant. The label weighs breastfeeding's benefits against the mother's need for FORZINITY and any possible harm to the infant (section 8.2). These findings come from FORZINITY's label; research-grade powder is a different product with no safety testing of its own. The MMPOWER-3 trial excluded pregnant or breastfeeding women and required highly effective birth control for women who could become pregnant (NCT03323749)

Severe renal impairment: a dose change, not a contraindication on the FORZINITY label. FORZINITY's dose is halved to 20 mg once daily for adults with eGFR under 30 mL/min who are not on dialysis (sections 2.2 and 8.6). Mild or moderate impairment needs no change. There is no labelled dose for adults on dialysis or for children with renal impairment. Elamipretide is excreted in the urine; exposure rose 125% in severe impairment (section 12.3)
Children under 30 kg: safety and effectiveness have not been established (section 8.4). The label dose is for patients 30 kg and up (section 2.1)

Newborns: the label says "Do not use in neonates" (section 5.1). FORZINITY contains 20 mg/mL benzyl alcohol as a preservative. Serious and fatal reactions, including gasping syndrome, have been reported in low-birth-weight and preterm newborns given benzyl alcohol-containing drugs intravenously (sections 5.1 and 8.4)

Active malignancy or history of cancer: a research caution, not on the FORZINITY label. No carcinogenicity studies have been done (label section 13.1), and MMPOWER-3 excluded active cancer or cancer within the past 2 years (NCT03323749)

Severe cardiac conduction abnormalities: a research caution, not on the FORZINITY label. MMPOWER-3 excluded most active conduction abnormalities (NCT03323749), so safety in this group is not established
Anthracycline chemotherapeutics (doxorubicin, daunorubicin): SS-31 may mask early signs of cardiotoxicity by protecting mitochondria; monitor cardiac function closely if co-administered
Other mitochondrial-targeted compounds (MitoQ, CoQ10, idebenone): no formal interaction studies; theoretical additive effects on mitochondrial membrane dynamics
Immunosuppressants (cyclosporine A): cyclosporine inhibits mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening, which overlaps with SS-31 mechanism; potential for unpredictable combined effects
Insulin and oral hypoglycemics: while SS-31 does not directly affect glucose metabolism, improved mitochondrial function may alter insulin sensitivity; monitor blood glucose
Anticoagulants: no known pharmacokinetic interaction, but as with all subcutaneous injectables, monitor for injection site bruising

SS-31 (elamipretide) received FDA accelerated approval on September 19, 2025 under the brand name FORZINITY (NDA 215244) for treatment of Barth syndrome in adults and pediatric patients weighing at least 30 kg. Continued approval is contingent on a confirmatory clinical trial verifying clinical benefit. FORZINITY is manufactured by Stealth BioTherapeutics. As of October 2026, Drugs@FDA lists no approval for any other indication, including heart failure. SS-31 has historically been sold as a research peptide under various names (SS-31, MTP-131, Bendavia). SS-31 is sold for research purposes only through non-pharmaceutical channels. It is not WADA-listed as of early 2026, though athletes should verify current prohibited substance lists before use. This content is for educational and informational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Consult a qualified healthcare provider before using any peptide.

phases.syringeUnits: 0.5 mL of the ready-to-use 80 mg/mL solution, drawn straight from the vial with nothing mixed in (label sections 2.1, 3 and 11); use only the syringe your healthcare provider prescribes (Instructions for Use)
phases.notes: FDA-approved dose for Barth syndrome in adults and pediatric patients ≥30 kg (label section 2.1). FORZINITY comes as a 280 mg/3.5 mL (80 mg/mL) single-patient-use vial and needs no reconstitution (section 3). Adults with severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min, not on dialysis): 20 mg once daily, 0.25 mL at 80 mg/mL (section 2.2). The label gives no dose for adults on dialysis or for children with renal impairment. Skip a missed dose and never double the next one (section 2.1). Inject into the abdomen, at least 2 inches from the navel, or the outer thigh, and rotate sites daily (section 2.3). Discard an opened vial 8 days after first opening (sections 2.3 and 16.2). It contains benzyl alcohol (20 mg/mL) and is not for use in neonates (sections 5.1 and 8.4).

protocols.duration: Continuous; continued approval contingent on confirmatory trial results
protocols.monitoringNotes: Monitor injection site reactions; manage with oral antihistamines or topical corticosteroids. CBC: eosinophilia occurs in majority ≥30 days of use, peaks ~day 90, typically resolves. Renal function monitoring given renal excretion pathway.

faqs.q: Why does the community use 1-10 mg when the FDA-approved dose is 40 mg?
faqs.a: The 4 mg dose was studied in early Phase 2 heart failure trials (EMBRACE-HF) alongside 40 mg and showed meaningful effects at the lower amount. Community users have latched onto this as a "minimum effective dose" concept, reasoning that healthy aging individuals need far less than patients with confirmed mitochondrial dysfunction. No dose-finding trial has been done in healthy adults though.

faqs.q: Did the TAZPOWER trial actually prove SS-31 works?
faqs.a: Not exactly. The primary endpoints (6-minute walk test, total fatigue score) were not met in the 12-week crossover. FDA accelerated approval was based on knee extensor muscle strength improvement seen in the open-label extension: an intermediate biomarker, not a clinical outcome. Continued approval depends on a confirmatory trial.

faqs.q: What are the injection site reactions like?
faqs.a: In TAZPOWER, 100% of participants had injection site redness, 75% had pain, and 67% had induration. That's the primary tolerability concern. Community reports say it gets more manageable after the first few weeks, and rotating sites helps. Eosinophilia also occurs in most users during the first 90 days but typically normalizes without symptoms.

faqs.q: What's the difference between ELZURA and FORZINITY?
faqs.a: The FDA-approved product as of September 2025 is FORZINITY (NDA 215244), not ELZURA. Some databases reference an "ELZURA" FDA label URL that returns a 404 error. Use NDA 215244 / FORZINITY for current prescribing information. FORZINITY is a ready-to-use 80 mg/mL solution in a 280 mg/3.5 mL vial, so it is never mixed with BAC water (label sections 3 and 11).

faqs.q: Is elamipretide safe for people with kidney disease?
faqs.a: The FDA label doesn't contraindicate it in renal impairment: it calls for a dose reduction to 20 mg/day for severe renal impairment (eGFR under 30, not on dialysis). That's a dose adjustment, not a contraindication. Standard renal function monitoring is appropriate.

Research-grade SS-31 comes as lyophilized powder in 5, 10 or 40 mg vials, mixed with bacteriostatic water. The calculator default, 0.5 mL in a 5 mg vial, gives 10 mg/mL. FORZINITY, the FDA-approved product, is never reconstituted. It is a ready-to-use 80 mg/mL solution. The 40 mg label dose is 0.5 mL, drawn straight from the vial (label sections 2.1, 3 and 11).

faqs.q: What is the half-life of SS-31 (Elamipretide)?
faqs.a: The half-life of SS-31 (Elamipretide) is ~4 hours. This determines how frequently you need to dose for consistent blood levels.

summary: FDA accelerated approval came through September 2025, making elamipretide one of only a handful of mitochondrial-targeted drugs to reach the market. SS-31 (brand name FORZINITY, also known as elamipretide, MTP-131, or Bendavia) is a four-amino-acid peptide that crosses into mitochondria and binds cardiolipin, a lipid that holds the electron transport chain together. The TAZPOWER trial earned approval based on knee extensor strength gains in Barth syndrome patients, though the randomized-phase primary endpoints were not met. Longevity researchers and biohackers now use SS-31 at community-derived doses between 2 and 10 mg daily for energy, recovery, and mitochondrial support.
